text: Lessons 2 through 8 closed the technical half of Lesson 1's gap: a real schedule, a confirmed backup chain, a tested restore, a health check. This lesson closes the other half — making sure what you know doesn't leave the building when you do. A plan that only lives in your head is exactly as fragile as the untested maintenance plan that started this whole project.

A real backup and restore runbook needs seven things: a system overview of what the database is and who depends on it, the real backup schedule, the retention window, the exact restore procedure, the date and result of the last tested restore, the health check from Lesson 8, and an escalation path for who to contact if something doesn't go as expected.

The last tested restore line deserves special attention — it's the single most important entry in the whole document, because it's the direct, written answer to Priya's original question from Lesson 1: has this actually been tested, and when.

The real test of a runbook isn't whether it reads well on a calm Tuesday — it's whether a stressed, unfamiliar teammate could follow it during an actual incident. That means exact commands, not descriptions. Run the restore CLI command is useless at 2 a.m. The actual az sql db restore command, with your real resource group, server, and database names already filled in, is what someone can actually use.

Go back to Lesson 1's final requirement: a short runbook anyone on the team could follow. Everything else in this capstone exists to make that document true and specific instead of aspirational. Writing it isn't a formality after the real work — it is the real work, made durable. Last lesson, you'll recap everything you built, and see what's next.
